`avoid_store_forwarding` is an x86-oriented performance pass that scans loads and stores in a basic block and tries to detect memory-access patterns that would cause a CPU store-to-load forwarding penalty. When it finds a problematic overlap or partial overlap, it may rewrite or reschedule the sequence to avoid the hardware hazard.

The backtrace shows the faulting routine is `(anonymous namespace)::store_forwarding_analyzer::is_store_forwarding(rtx_def*, rtx_def*, long*)` in `avoid-store-forwarding.cc:152`. Specifically: (1) The code will always be a comparison operation (EQ, NE, GT, etc.). (2) Both operands will be machine operands. (3) If an operand is a constant, it will be the second operand. Return the number of bytes to "protect" on the stack for -fstack-check. gcc/explow.cc.summary: Emit the end of a stack clash probing loop. This consists of just the jump back to LOOP_LAB and emitting END_LOOP after the loop.

Adjust the stack pointer by minus SIZE (an rtx for a number of bytes) while probing it. This pushes when SIZE is positive. SIZE need not be constant. This is subtly different than anti_adjust_stack_and_probe to try and prevent stack-clash attacks 1. It must assume no knowledge of the probing state, any allocation must probe. Consider the case of a 1 byte alloca in a loop. If the sum of the allocations is large, then this could be used to jump the guard if probes were not emitted. 2. It never skips probes, whereas anti_adjust_stack_and_probe will skip the probe on the first PROBE_INTERVAL on the assumption it was already done in the prologue and in previous allocations. 3. It only allocates and probes SIZE bytes, it does not need to allocate/probe beyond that because this probing style does not guarantee signal handling capability if the guard is hit.
